{{short description|Mathematical concept}}
{{See Wiktionary}}

In [[mathematics]], especially in the area of [[abstract algebra]] that studies [[infinite group]]s, the adverb '''virtually''' is used to modify a property so that it need only hold for a [[subgroup]] of finite [[Index of a subgroup|index]].  Given a property P, the group ''G'' is said to be ''virtually P'' if there is a finite index subgroup <math>H \le G</math> such that ''H'' has property P.

Common uses for this would be when P is [[Abelian group|abelian]], [[Nilpotent group|nilpotent]], [[solvable group|solvable]] or [[Free group|free]]. For example, virtually solvable groups are one of the two alternatives in the [[Tits alternative]], while [[Gromov's theorem on groups of polynomial growth|Gromov's theorem]] states that the finitely generated groups with [[Growth rate (group theory)|polynomial growth]] are precisely the finitely generated virtually nilpotent groups.

This terminology is also used when P is just another group.  That is, if ''G'' and ''H'' are groups then ''G'' is ''virtually'' ''H'' if ''G'' has a subgroup ''K'' of finite index in ''G'' such that ''K'' is [[isomorphism|isomorphic]] to ''H''.

In particular, a group is virtually trivial if and only if it is finite. Two groups are virtually equal if and only if they are [[Commensurability (group theory)|commensurable]].

==Examples ==

===Virtually abelian===
The following groups are virtually abelian.
*Any abelian group.
*Any [[semidirect product]] <math>N\rtimes H</math> where ''N'' is abelian and ''H'' is finite. (For example, any [[generalized dihedral group]].)
*Any semidirect product <math>N\rtimes H</math> where ''N'' is finite and ''H'' is abelian.
*Any finite group (since the trivial subgroup is abelian).

===Virtually nilpotent===
*Any group that is virtually abelian.
*Any nilpotent group.
*Any semidirect product <math>N\rtimes H</math> where ''N'' is nilpotent and ''H'' is finite.
*Any semidirect product <math>N\rtimes H</math> where ''N'' is finite and ''H'' is nilpotent.

[[Gromov's theorem on groups of polynomial growth|Gromov's theorem]] says that a finitely generated group is virtually nilpotent if and only if it has polynomial growth.

===Virtually polycyclic===
{{main|virtually polycyclic group}}

===Virtually free===
*Any [[free group]].
*Any finite group (since the trivial subgroup is the free group on the empty set of generators).
*Any virtually [[cyclic group]]. (Either it is finite in which case it falls into the above case, or it is infinite and contains <math>\Z</math> as a subgroup.)
*Any semidirect product <math>N\rtimes H</math> where ''N'' is free and ''H'' is finite.
*Any semidirect product <math>N\rtimes H</math> where ''N'' is finite and ''H'' is free.
*Any [[free product]] <math>H*K</math>, where ''H'' and ''K'' are both finite. (For example, the [[modular group]] <math>\operatorname{PSL}(2,\Z)</math>.)

It follows from [[Stallings theorem about ends of groups#Applications and generalizations|Stalling's theorem]] that any torsion-free virtually free group is free.

===Others===
The free group <math>F_2</math> on 2 generators is virtually <math>F_n</math> for any <math>n\ge  2</math> as a consequence of the [[Nielsen–Schreier theorem]] and the [[Schreier index formula]].

The group <math>\operatorname{O}(n)</math> is virtually connected as <math>\operatorname{SO}(n)</math> has index 2 in it.
